registryLegalName: Petition for Expungement Where Another Person Used the Petitioner's Identity, Va. Code § 19.2-392.2(B)

primaryStatutoryAuthority.description: If any person whose name or other identification has been used without his consent or authorisation by another person who has been charged or arrested using such name or identification, he may file a petition with the court disposing of the charge for relief under the section, without paying any court fees or costs. The petition shall include one complete set of the petitioner's fingerprints obtained from a law-enforcement agency.

Prescribes the proof route: the petitioner obtains the fingerprint set from a law-enforcement agency and gives that agency a copy of the petition; the agency submits the fingerprints to the Central Criminal Records Exchange with the petition attached; the CCRE forwards the criminal history and the fingerprint set to the court under seal. On completion of the hearing the court returns the fingerprint card, and where no hearing was held the card is destroyed unless the petitioner asks for it back within thirty days or supplies a stamped self-addressed envelope.

Supplies a distinct and faster route where the charge is dismissed because the court finds the person arrested or charged is not the person named in the summons, warrant, indictment or presentment: the dismissing court, on motion of the person improperly charged, enters the expungement order.

counselFlags: Two routes, and the faster one may be correct: § 19.2-392.2(H) supplies a distinct and faster route where the charge is dismissed because the court finds the person arrested or charged is not the person named in the summons, warrant, indictment or presentment — there the dismissing court enters the expungement order on motion of the person improperly charged. Whether that motion has its own instrument is part of the unresolved form question. Screening must not push a participant onto the (B) petition where (H) fits.

Fingerprints and the CCRE route are prescribed by § 19.2-392.2(E) and involve third parties: the petitioner obtains a complete set of fingerprints from a law-enforcement agency and gives that agency a copy of the petition; the agency submits the fingerprints to the Central Criminal Records Exchange with the petition attached; the CCRE forwards the criminal history and fingerprint set to the court under seal. LegalEase never asserts that any of those steps has been performed.

Fingerprint card handling: on completion of the hearing the court returns the fingerprint card, and where no hearing was held the card is destroyed unless the petitioner asks for it back within thirty days or supplies a stamped self-addressed envelope. A participant must be told this before filing.

No verification or notarization statute is identified for a § 19.2-392.2(B) petition, and verification is in any event a feature of whatever official form governs the route — which is the unresolved question. Nothing is filled.
Fee: § 19.2-392.2(B) provides that the petition is filed without paying any court fees or costs. That is a statutory exemption rather than an amount, and no amount may be stated to a participant.

Form status unresolved: the only Virginia expungement form obtained, CC-1473, is captioned to § 19.2-392.2(A) alone and does not support this route; other circuit-court expungement forms were not retrievable from the official library on 2026-08-06 (HTTP 404). Whether a subsection (B) form exists is unknown.

Registry release blocker (open): Chapter 23.2 and § 19.2-392.2 both carry future versions that the controlling review predates and does not record. The subsection lettering relied on here may shift between versions, so any instrument must be rebuilt against the version in force at build time.
No waiting period applies: § 19.2-392.2(B) imposes none. Venue is the court disposing of the charge, and on the subsection (H) route the order is entered by the court dismissing the charge.

dependencies.barsDraftingBecause: Virginia circuit-court expungement runs on Supreme Court of Virginia forms, and one such form (CC-1473) demonstrably exists for the adjacent subsection. Drafting a custom § 19.2-392.2(B) petition would either replicate an official form that exists but was not retrievable, or invent an instrument for a route the state may already have formalised. The 404s establish that the library was not fully readable on the retrieval date, not that no form exists.
